claim: Radial growth in plants is mediated by the cambium, a stem cell niche continuously producing wood (xylem) and bast (phloem) in a strictly bidirectional manner.
source: In plants, radial growth is mediated by the cambium, a stem cell niche continuously producing wood (xylem) and bast (phloem) in a strictly bidirectional manner.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract and is supported by established scientific knowledge about plant anatomy.

claim: Cambium dynamics eludes direct experimental access due to obstacles in live-cell imaging.
source: While this process contributes large parts to terrestrial biomass, cambium dynamics eludes direct experimental access due to obstacles in live-cell imaging.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a rationale for the computational modeling approach.

claim: The receptor-like kinase PXY and its ligand CLE41 are part of a minimal framework sufficient for instructing tissue organization.
source: Performing iterative comparisons of plant and model anatomies, we conclude that the receptor-like kinase PXY and its ligand CLE41 are part of a minimal framework sufficient for instructing tissue organization.
evidence: This conclusion is based on computational modeling results compared with experimental observations.

claim: A limited number of factors are sufficient to create radial growth by bidirectional tissue production.
source: Our model highlights the role of intercellular communication within the cambium and shows that a limited number of factors are sufficient to create radial growth by bidirectional tissue production.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the computational modeling results presented in the study.

claim: Cambium cells are embedded in two distinct vascular tissues produced in opposite directions by periclinal cell divisions: xylem (wood) and phloem (bast).
source: Cambium cells are embedded in two distinct vascular tissues produced in opposite directions by periclinal cell divisions: xylem (wood) and phloem (bast) (Chiang and Greb, 2019; Haas et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Xylem carries out long-distance transport of water and nutrients.
source: These tissues carry out fundamental physiological functions: long-distance transport of water and nutrients in case of the xylem and translocation of sugars and a multitude of signaling molecules in the case of the phloem.
evidence: This is established knowledge about plant vascular tissue function.

claim: Phloem carries out translocation of sugars and a multitude of signaling molecules.
source: These tissues carry out fundamental physiological functions: long-distance transport of water and nutrients in case of the xylem and translocation of sugars and a multitude of signaling molecules in the case of the phloem.
evidence: This is established knowledge about plant vascular tissue function.

claim: The cambium is a paradigm for bifacial stem cell niches which produce two tissue types in opposite directions and are found across different kingdoms of life.
source: Based on its tightly controlled bidirectionality of tissue production and resulting bipartite organization, the cambium is a paradigm for bifacial stem cell niches which produce two tissue types in opposite directions and are found across different kingdoms of life (Shi et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Early xylem cells instruct radial patterning of the cambium, including stem cell activity, and fulfill this role only transiently.
source: During their transition from stem cells to fully differentiated xylem cells, early xylem cells instruct radial patterning of the cambium, including stem cell activity and, thus, similar to the OC in the SAM, fulfill this role only transiently (Smetana et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Phloem-derived DOF transcription factors designated as PHLOEM EARLY DOFs (PEARs) move to cambium stem cells and stimulate their proliferation in a non-cell-autonomous manner.
source: In addition to influence from the early xylem, phloem-derived DNA-BINDING ONE ZINC FINGER (DOF) transcription factors designated as PHLOEM EARLY DOFs (PEARs) move to cambium stem cells and stimulate their proliferation in a non-cell-autonomous manner (Miyashima et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Cell divisions are mostly restricted to individual bifacial stem cells located in the central cambium feeding both xylem and phloem production.
source: Furthermore, genetically encoded lineage-tracing experiments showed that cell divisions are mostly restricted to individual bifacial stem cells located in the central cambium feeding both xylem and phloem production (Smetana et al., 2019; Shi et al., 2019; Bossinger and Spokevicius, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The receptor-ligand pair formed by PXY and CLE41/CLE44 peptides is a central mechanism regulating cambium activity in Arabidopsis thaliana and beyond.
source: Another central and well-established mechanism regulating cambium activity in the reference plant Arabidopsis thaliana and beyond (Kucukoglu et al., 2017; Etchells and Turner, 2010; Etchells et al., 2015; Fisher and Turner, 2007) is the action of a receptor-ligand pair formed by the plasma membrane-bound receptor-like kinase PHLOEM INTERCALATED WITH XYLEM (PXY), also known as TDIF RECEPTOR (TDR), and the secreted CLAVATA3/ESR-RELATED 41 (CLE41) and CLE44 peptides.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: CLE41 and CLE44 are expressed in the phloem and thought to diffuse to dividing cells in the cambium area expressing PXY.
source: Like the PEAR proteins (Miyashima et al., 2019), CLE41 and CLE44 are expressed in the phloem and thought to diffuse to dividing cells in the cambium area expressing PXY (Etchells and Turner, 2010; Hirakawa et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Direct binding of CLE41 to PXY promotes the expression of the transcription factor WOX4.
source: Direct binding of CLE41 to PXY (Hirakawa et al., 2008; Morita et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2016) promotes the expression of the transcription factor WUSCHEL RELATED HOMEOBOX 4 (WOX4) (Hirakawa et al., 2010), which, in turn, is crucial for maintaining the capacity of cells to proliferate (Kucukoglu et al., 2017; Hirakawa et al., 2010; Suer et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: WOX4 is crucial for maintaining the capacity of cells to proliferate.
source: Direct binding of CLE41 to PXY (Hirakawa et al., 2008; Morita et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2016) promotes the expression of the transcription factor WUSCHEL RELATED HOMEOBOX 4 (WOX4) (Hirakawa et al., 2010), which, in turn, is crucial for maintaining the capacity of cells to proliferate (Kucukoglu et al., 2017; Hirakawa et al., 2010; Suer et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The PXY/CLE41 module represses xylem differentiation in a WOX4-independent manner.
source: At the same time, the PXY/CLE41 module is reported to repress xylem differentiation in a WOX4-independent manner (Hirakawa et al., 2010; Kondo et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: PXY stimulates the activity of glycogen synthase kinase 3 proteins (GSK3s), like BIN2.
source: In this context, PXY stimulates the activity of glycogen synthase kinase 3 proteins (GSK3s), like BRASSINOSTEROID-INSENSITIVE 2 (BIN2) (Kondo et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: BIN2 represses the transcriptional regulator BES1, which mediates brassinosteroid (BR) signaling and promotes xylem differentiation.
source: BIN2, in turn, represses the transcriptional regulator BRI1-EMS SUPPRESSOR 1 (BES1), which mediates brassinosteroid (BR) signaling and promotes xylem differentiation (Kondo et al., 2014; Saito et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: PXY is expressed in the proximal cambium zone containing developing xylem cells and in the central cambium zone containing bifacial cambium stem cells.
source: In line with the hypothesis of a dual role in regulating stem cell activity and xylem differentiation, PXY is expressed in the proximal cambium zone containing developing xylem cells and in the central cambium zone containing bifacial cambium stem cells (Shi et al., 2019; Brackmann et al., 2018; Shi et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: MOL1 represses cambium activity.
source: Distally to the PXY expression domain and oriented towards the phloem, the closest homolog to PXY, the receptor-like kinase MORE LATERAL GROWTH 1 (MOL1), represses cambium activity (Agusti et al., 2011b; Gursanscky et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: PXY and MOL1 cannot functionally replace each other, indicating that MOL1 activity does not depend on CLE41/44 peptides.
source: Although their extracellular domains are highly similar, PXY and MOL1 cannot functionally replace each other, indicating that MOL1 activity does not depend on CLE41/44 peptides and that distinct signaling loops act in the proximal and distal cambium domains (Gursanscky et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: ARF5 is expressed in the proximal cambium and promotes the transition from stem cells to xylem cells by directly dampening WOX4 activity.
source: The latter conclusion is supported by the finding that the AUXIN RESPONSE FACTOR5 (ARF5) is expressed in the proximal cambium and promotes the transition from stem cells to xylem cells by directly dampening WOX4 activity (Brackmann et al., 2018; Han et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: ARF5 activity is enhanced by phosphorylation through BIL1, which is inhibited by the PXY/CLE41 module.
source: ARF5 activity is enhanced by phosphorylation through the GSK3 BIN2-LIKE 1 (BIL1) which, in contrast to other GSK3s (Kondo et al., 2014), is inhibited by the PXY/CLE41 module (Han et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Model 1 maintained a circular pool of dividing cambium cells* with a high concentration of PXYactive* while producing xylem cells* toward the center of the organ.
source: In the resulting Model 1, the growing structure maintained a circular pool of dividing cambium cells* with a high concentration of PXYactive* while producing xylem cells* toward the center of the organ (Figure 1C, Videos 1–4).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the computational model output shown in Figure 1C and associated videos.

claim: In Model 1, cambium cells* displaced to the proximal side of the cambium* stopped dividing likely due to low [PXYactive*].
source: As expected, when cambium cells* were displaced to the proximal side of the cambium*, they stopped dividing likely due to low [PXYactive*] (Figure 1C and D, Video 3, Video 4, Video 5) allowing them to reach a size sufficient for xylem* differentiation.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the computational model output shown in Figure 1C and D and associated videos.

claim: In Model 1, cell* division rates were highest close to CLE41* producing phloem cells*.
source: Cell* division rates were highest close to CLE41* producing phloem cells* (Figure 1D–G, Video 2, Video 3).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the computational model output shown in Figure 1D-G and associated videos.

claim: In Model 1, [PXY*] was particularly low in the distal cambium* region.
source: Moreover, as PXYactive* negatively affected the production of PXY*, [PXY*] was particularly low in the distal cambium* region (Figure 1C, F and G. Video 1, Video 5).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the computational model output shown in Figure 1C, F, and G and associated videos.

claim: The pattern of [PXY*] in Model 1 was reminiscent of the exclusive activity of the PXY promoter in the proximal cambium area observed previously.
source: This pattern was reminiscent of the exclusive activity of the PXY promoter in the proximal cambium area observed previously (Shi et al., 2019; Gursanscky et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a comparison between model output and previously published experimental observations.

claim: Model 2A produced a descending gradient of cell* division rates in the distal cambium* domain likely due to high levels of PXYactive*.
source: The computational implementation of these rules (Model 2A) resulted in a descending gradient of cell* division rates in the distal cambium* domain likely due to high levels of PXYactive* (Figure 2B–E, Video 6, Video 7, Video 8).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the computational model output shown in Figure 2B-E and associated videos.

claim: In Model 2A, the cell* division rate was highest in the central cambium* domain defined by high [PXY*] and by moderate [PXYactive*].
source: The cell* division rate was highest in the central cambium* domain defined by high [PXY*] and by moderate [PXYactive*] (Figure 2B–D, Video 8, Video 9, Video 10, Video 11).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the computational model output shown in Figure 2B-D and associated videos.

claim: Model 2A continuously produced both xylem* and phloem*, and the fate of cambium cells* was dependent on their position relative to the differentiated tissues*.
source: Also, not only xylem* but also phloem* was continuously produced and the fate of cambium cells* was dependent on their position relative to the differentiated tissues*.
evidence: This is a description of the behavior of Model 2A.

claim: In Model 2A, cells* in the central cambium* domain proliferated and constantly replenished the stem cell pool.
source: In the central cambium* domain, cells* proliferated and constantly replenished the stem cell pool (Figure 2B, Video 6, Video 7, Video 8).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the computational model output shown in Figure 2B and associated videos.

claim: Model 2A reproduced the anatomy of a mature Arabidopsis hypocotyl in qualitative terms.
source: Thus, by incorporating relatively simple rules, Model 2A comprised major cambium features, including phloem formation. Moreover, in qualitative terms, the resulting anatomy* reproduced the anatomy of a mature Arabidopsis hypocotyl (Figure 2A and E).
evidence: This is a comparison between model output (Figure 2E) and experimental observations (Figure 2A).

claim: The cambium* in Model 2A displayed a clear front instability, suggesting that a stabilizing mechanism exists that was missed in the model.
source: It is interesting to note, however, while the cambium domain stays almost perfectly circular in plants, the cambium* in our simulations displayed a clear front instability, suggesting that a stabilizing mechanism exists that we missed in our model.
evidence: This is an inference based on the discrepancy between model behavior and observed plant anatomy.

claim: Ectopic expression of CLE41 by employing the IRX3 promoter substantially alters hypocotyl anatomy.
source: Ectopic expression of CLE41 by employing the IRREGULAR XYLEM 3/CELLULOSE SYNTHASE CATALYTIC SUBUNIT 7 (IRX3/CESA7) promoter, which is active in cells undergoing secondary cell wall deposition (Mitsuda et al., 2007; Taylor et al., 2003; Smith et al., 2013), substantially alters hypocotyl anatomy (Etchells and Turner, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: In IRX3pro:CLE41 plants, PXYpro:CFP activity was found in irregularly shaped patches containing differentiated xylem vessel elements distributed over the whole cross-section.
source: While in the presence of the IRX3pro:CLE41 transgene, PXYpro:CFP activity was found in irregularly shaped patches containing differentiated xylem vessel elements distributed over the whole cross-section (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1, Figure 3—figure supplement 2, Figure 3—figure supplement 3, Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental observations shown in Figure 3A and supplementary figures.

claim: In IRX3pro:CLE41 plants, regions without PXYpro:CFP activity in proximal hypocotyl regions showed SMXL5pro:YFP activity.
source: Moreover, we observed regions without PXYpro:CFP activity in proximal hypocotyl regions where SMXL5pro:YFP was active (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1, Figure 3—figure supplement 2, Figure 3—figure supplement 3, Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental observations shown in Figure 3A and supplementary figures.

claim: In IRX3pro:CLE41 plants, a substantial part of SMXL5pro:YFP activity was detected in the distal regions of the hypocotyl forming islands of irregular shape sometimes intermingled with PXYpro:CFP activity.
source: Besides, a substantial part of SMXL5pro:YFP activity was detected in the distal regions of the hypocotyl forming islands of irregular shape sometimes intermingled with PXYpro:CFP activity (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1, Figure 3—figure supplement 2, Figure 3—figure supplement 3, Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental observations shown in Figure 3A and supplementary figures.

claim: Not only the radial symmetry of the hypocotyl but also cambium organization depends on the site of CLE41 production.
source: These results indicated that not only the radial symmetry of the hypocotyl (Etchells and Turner, 2010) but also cambium organization depends on the site of CLE41 production.
evidence: This is an inference based on experimental observations of IRX3pro:CLE41 plants.

claim: In Model 2B, xylem* formation was initially repressed possibly due to high levels of PXYactive* in all cambium* cells.
source: Although in this case xylem* formation was initially repressed possibly due to high levels of PXYactive* in all cambium* cells (Figure 3B, Video 12, Video 13, Video 14), new xylem cells* were formed as soon as the distance between existing xylem and phloem cells* became large enough such that CLE41* levels and, in turn, [PXYactive*] dropped to permissive levels (Figure 3C, Video 12, Video 13, Video 14).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the computational model output shown in Figure 3B and C and associated videos.

claim: In Model 2B, new phloem cells* were produced close to existing phloem and xylem cells* likely due to high levels of PXYactive*.
source: New phloem cells* were produced close to existing phloem and xylem cells* likely due to high levels of PXYactive* (Figure 3C, Video 15, Video 16).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the computational model output shown in Figure 3C and associated videos.

claim: Model 2B produced a similar disruption in cambium* organization as observed in IRX3pro:CLE41 plants.
source: As a result, Model 2B produced a similar disruption in cambium* organization, as observed in IRX3pro:CLE41 plants (Figure 3D, Video 12, Video 13, Video 14).
evidence: This is a comparison between model output (Figure 3D) and experimental observations.

claim: In Model 2B, zones with both high [PXYactive*] and low [PXY*] appeared in the organ* center together with individual xylem cells*.
source: Zones with both high [PXYactive*] and low [PXY*], which were found in the distal cambium* in Model 2A (Figure 2E, Video 16, Video 17), appeared in the organ* center together with individual xylem cells* (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the computational model output shown in Figure 3D.

claim: In Model 2B, new phloem cells* were produced in the central areas of the organ* as demonstrated previously for IRX3pro:CLE41 plants.
source: Moreover, in addition to being produced in distal regions, new phloem cells* were produced in the central areas of the organ* as demonstrated previously for IRX3pro:CLE41 plants (Etchells and Turner, 2010).
evidence: This is a comparison between model output and previously published experimental observations.

claim: Rules determining cambium* polarity implemented in Model 2 were sufficient to simulate organ anatomy found in wild-type and IRX3pro:CLE41 genetic backgrounds.
source: Thus, rules determining cambium* polarity implemented in Model 2 were sufficient to simulate organ anatomy found in wild-type and IRX3pro:CLE41 genetic backgrounds.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the comparison of model outputs with experimental observations.

claim: In pxy mutants, the xylem tissue did not have a cylindrical shape, but was instead clustered in radial sectors showing PXYpro:CFP and SMXL5pro:YFP activity.
source: In pxy mutants, the xylem tissue did not have a cylindrical shape, but was instead clustered in radial sectors showing PXYpro:CFP and, at their distal ends, SMXL5pro:YFP activity, whereas regions in between those sectors had little to no xylem and did not show reporter activity (Figure 3E, Figure 2—figure supplement 1, Figure 3—figure supplement 1, Figure 3—figure supplement 2, Figure 3—figure supplement 3, Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental observations shown in Figure 3E and supplementary figures.

claim: In pxy mutants, PXYpro:CFP and SMXL5pro:YFP activity domains were still mostly distinct, meaning that PXYpro:CFP activity did not expand further beyond established xylem than in wild type.
source: Interestingly, PXYpro:CFP and SMXL5pro:YFP activity domains were still mostly distinct meaning that PXYpro:CFP activity did not expand further beyond established xylem than in wild type (Figure 3E, Figure 3—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental observations shown in Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 5.

claim: The CLE41-PXY signaling module did not restrict PXY promoter activity in the distal cambium.
source: This discrepancy indicated that, in contrast to our assumption, the CLE41-PXY signaling module did not restrict PXY promoter activity in the distal cambium.
evidence: This is an inference based on the discrepancy between model predictions and experimental observations in pxy mutants.

claim: The sharp border between PXYpro:CFP and SMXL5pro:YFP activity was less pronounced in pxy mutants mostly due to a spread of SMXL5pro:YFP activity towards xylem tissues.
source: Of note, the sharp border between PXYpro:CFP and SMXL5pro:YFP activity was less pronounced in pxy mutants mostly due to a spread of SMXL5pro:YFP activity towards xylem tissues (Figure 3—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental observations shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 5.

claim: Completely eliminating PXY* activity from the model (Model 2C) resulted in the absence of growth due to the full dependence of cell* divisions on the PXY* function.
source: The discrepancy between Model 2 and the situation in plants was confirmed when we completely eliminated PXY* activity from our model (Model 2C). As expected, this elimination resulted in the absence of growth due to the full dependence of cell* divisions on the PXY* function, clearly being at odds with the phenotype of pxy mutants (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the computational model output and comparison with experimental observations.

claim: Reducing PXY* activity (Model 2D) did not result in a split of the continuous cambium domain* but abolished phloem* formation and increased the production of xylem*.
source: Even when we only reduced PXY* activity (Model 2D), this did not result in a split of the continuous cambium domain* but abolished phloem* formation and increased the production of xylem* (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the computational model output shown in Figure 3F.

claim: The total number of xylem cells and the number of xylem vessels was comparable between wild-type and pxy mutant hypocotyls.
source: Interestingly, the quantification of water transporting xylem vessels, xylem fibers, which provide mechanical stability, and xylem parenchyma in sections from wild-type and pxy mutant hypocotyls by automated image segmentation revealed that the total number of xylem cells and the number of xylem vessels was comparable (Figure 3G–I, Figure 3—figure supplement 6).
evidence: This is demonstrated by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 3G-I and Figure 3—figure supplement 6.

claim: The number of cells classified as fibers was substantially reduced in pxy mutants, whereas the number of cells classified as parenchyma was increased.
source: In contrast, the number of cells classified as fibers was substantially reduced in pxy mutants, whereas the number of cells classified as parenchyma was increased (Figure 3G–I).
evidence: This is demonstrated by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 3G-I.

claim: During radial growth PXY promotes the fiber-parenchyma ratio in the xylem, while the formation of xylem vessels and the total number of cambium-derived cells produced toward the xylem is hardly PXY-dependent.
source: These results suggested that during radial growth PXY promotes the fiber-parenchyma ratio in the xylem, while the formation of xylem vessels and the total number of cambium-derived cells produced toward the xylem is hardly PXY-dependent.
evidence: This is an inference based on the quantitative analysis of wild-type and pxy mutant hypocotyls.

claim: Model 3A established two cambium* subdomains – the distal subdomain characterized by high concentrations of DF* and the proximal subdomain characterized by high PXY* concentration.
source: The implementation of these principles in silico (Model 3A) resulted again in the establishment of two cambium* subdomains – the distal subdomain that was characterized by high concentrations of DF* and the proximal subdomain characterized by high PXY* concentration (Figure 4B–D, Figure 4—figure supplement 1, Video 18, Video 19, Video 20, Video 21, Video 22, Video 23).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the computational model output shown in Figure 4B-D and associated videos.

claim: In Model 3A, the cambium* produced phloem parenchyma cells* from which phloem poles* were continuously formed with a pattern resembling the patchy phloem pattern observed in plants.
source: Distally, the cambium* produced phloem parenchyma cells* from which phloem poles* were continuously formed with a pattern resembling the patchy phloem pattern observed in plants (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1; Sankar et al., 2014; Wallner et al., 2020).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the computational model output shown in Figure 4B and comparison with cited literature.

claim: In Model 3A, the localization of PF* production mainly in phloem poles* resulted in increased DF levels in the vicinity of those poles and, consequently, in locally increased cell* division rates.
source: Interestingly, the localization of PF* production mainly in phloem poles* resulted in increased DF levels in the vicinity of those poles and, consequently, in locally increased cell* division rates (Video 20, Video 21).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the computational model output shown in associated videos.

claim: Phloem poles drive cell divisions in their immediate environment and phloem cells still divide after initial specification.
source: This observation is in line with the observation that phloem poles drive cell divisions in their immediate environment and that phloem cells still divide after initial specification (Miyashima et al., 2019; Bossinger and Spokevicius, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Patterns of PXY* and DF* in Model 3A were stable over time, comparable to the in planta situation.
source: When comparing the radial pattern of PXYpro:CFP/SMXL5pro:YFP activities and, as an in silico approximation to these activities, the distribution of PXY* and DF* in our model over time, patterns were stable in both cases (Figure 4B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1, Figure 3—figure supplement 2, Figure 3—figure supplement 3, Figure 3—figure supplement 4, Video 18, Video 22, Video 23).
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparison of model output with experimental observations over time.

claim: Model 3A was able to generate stable radial patterns of gene* activity comparable to the in planta situation.
source: This demonstrated that our model was able to generate stable radial patterns of gene* activity comparable to the in planta situation.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the comparison of model output with experimental observations.

claim: In Model 3B, CLE41* interacted with PXY* on the proximal cambium* border, which resulted in ectopic DF* production and phloem-parenchyma* formation in the proximal hypocotyl* regions.
source: By instructing CLE41* production additionally in xylem cells*, we next simulated CLE41-misexpression by the IRX3 promoter (Model 3B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1, Figure 4E, Video 24, Video 25, Video 26, Video 27, Video 28, Video 29). CLE41* interacted with PXY* on the proximal cambium* border, which resulted in ectopic DF* production and phloem-parenchyma* formation in the proximal hypocotyl* regions (Figure 4E, Video 24, Video 28), similarly as during radial hypocotyl growth in IRX3pro:CLE41 plants (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1, Figure 3—figure supplement 2, Figure 3—figure supplement 3, Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the computational model output shown in Figure 4E and associated videos, and comparison with experimental observations.

claim: Model 3B generated a patchy xylem* pattern resembling the xylem configuration found in IRX3pro:CLE41 plants.
source: Still, xylem cells* were formed, generating a patchy xylem* pattern resembling the xylem configuration found in IRX3pro:CLE41 plants (Figure 3A, Figure 4E, Video 24).
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparison of model output (Figure 4E) with experimental observations (Figure 3A).

claim: Fully eliminating CLE41* binding to PXY* (Model 3C) generated a patchy outline of the distal cambium* subdomain.
source: Fully eliminating CLE41* binding to PXY* and therefore PXY* activity but keeping the positional information of PXY* for xylem cell differentiation (Model 3C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1) generated a patchy outline of the distal cambium* subdomain (Figure 4F, Video 30, Video 31, Video 32, Video 33, Video 34, Video 35).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the computational model output shown in Figure 4F and associated videos.

claim: In Model 3C, PF* was sufficient for triggering cell divisions next to phloem poles*.
source: While PXY* was usually the main trigger of cell* divisions in cambium cells* at a certain distance from phloem poles*, PF* was sufficient for triggering cell divisions next to phloem poles*.
evidence: This is a description of the behavior of Model 3C.

claim: Heterogeneous cambium activity in Model 3C was already observable at early phases of radial hypocotyl growth in silico and in planta and resulted overall in a reduced tissue production in both systems.
source: Heterogeneous cambium activity was already observable at early phases of radial hypocotyl growth in silico and in planta and resulted overall in a reduced tissue production in both systems (Figure 4F, Figure 3—figure supplement 1, Figure 3—figure supplement 2, Figure 3—figure supplement 3, Figure 3—figure supplement 4, Video 30, Video 31, Video 32, Video 33, Video 34, Video 35).
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparison of model output with experimental observations.

claim: By introducing both a PXY*-independent pathway stimulating cambium* proliferation and a dependence of cell* proliferation on the distance to phloem poles*, the model was able to simulate important features of the pxy mutant phenotype.
source: Thus, by introducing both a PXY*-independent pathway stimulating cambium* proliferation and a dependence of cell* proliferation on the distance to phloem poles*, we were able to simulate important features of the pxy mutant phenotype (Figure 3E, Figure 4F, Figure 3—figure supplement 1, Figure 3—figure supplement 2, Figure 3—figure supplement 3, Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the comparison of model output with experimental observations.

claim: A computational cambium model sufficiently robust to simulate major genetic perturbations of cambium regulation was established.
source: Collectively, we concluded that we established a computational cambium model sufficiently robust to simulate major genetic perturbations of cambium regulation.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the successful simulation of multiple genetic perturbations.

claim: Cell division orientation in the model outputs was almost random, suggesting that radial cell file formation cannot be explained by the molecular signaling pathways implemented into the model.
source: Interestingly, although the overall tissue anatomy of the modeled organ* resembled the in planta situation, cell division orientation in our model outputs was almost random, suggesting that radial cell file formation cannot be explained by the molecular signaling pathways implemented into the model (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is an inference based on the discrepancy between model behavior and observed plant anatomy.

claim: The strong dominance of periclinal divisions in planta implies the presence of a positional signal instructing cell division orientation.
source: The strong dominance of periclinal divisions in planta, however, implies the presence of a positional signal instructing cell division orientation.
evidence: This is an inference based on observed plant anatomy.

claim: Classical observations indicated that physical forces play a role in cell division orientation.
source: Because classical observations indicated that physical forces play a role in this regard (Brown, 1964; Brown and Sax, 1962; Lintilhac and Vesecky, 1984), we tested whether the model was suited for finding indications for the influence of differential cell stiffness on geometric features of radial plant growth.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Staining intensities of cell wall dyes in cambium cells were approximately half as strong compared to cells of the surrounding tissue.
source: To do so, we first determined the relative cell wall thickness in hypocotyl cross-sections using the cell wall dyes Direct Yellow 96 and Direct Red 23 (Ursache et al., 2018) as an indication. Notably, staining intensities were approximately half as strong compared to cells of the surrounding tissue (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental observations shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Cambium stem cells are half as stiff as surrounding cells.
source: Expecting that staining intensities correlate with cell wall stiffness and by also taking into account results obtained previously by atomic force microscopy of the cambium region (Arnould et al., 2022), we assumed that cambium stem cells are half as stiff as surrounding cells and integrated this feature into our model by expanding VirtualLeaf to allow for the integration of cell-type specific wall stiffness (see Supporting Information 'VirtualLeaf Simulations' for details).
evidence: This is an assumption based on experimental observations and cited literature.

claim: Performing 12,500 simulations resulted in n = 5 parameter sets which produced more realistic cell-type proportions than achieved by manually selected parameters.
source: Performing 12,500 simulations resulted in n = 5 parameter sets (Supplementary file 2), which produced more realistic cell-type proportions than we achieved by our manually selected set before (Figure 4G, Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the automated parameter search results shown in Figure 4G and Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: By generating several parameter sets that described the experimentally observed tissue ratios equally well, the model behavior remained consistent reaffirming the model structure.
source: Furthermore, by generating several parameter sets that described the experimentally observed tissue ratios equally well, we demonstrated that even with differing parameter values the model behavior remained consistent reaffirming the model structure we had identified with Model 3A and was parameterized in Model 4 (Figure 5A and B, Figure 4—figure supplement 3, Video 36, Video 37, Video 38, Video 39, Video 40, Video 41).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the consistency of model behavior across different parameter sets.

claim: Increasing cell wall* stiffness led to a xylem*-specific decrease in cell* size and major axis length.
source: First we explored how the variation of the stiffness of xylem cell walls* impacted tissue formation (Figure 5C, Video 42, Video 43, Video 44, Video 45, Video 46, Video 47), we first observed that, as expected, increasing cell wall* stiffness led to a xylem*-specific decrease in cell* size and major axis length (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the computational model output shown in Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: Some cambium cells showed an increase in length as the cell type* with the closest proximity to xylem cells* when xylem cell wall* stiffness was increased.
source: In turn, some cambium cells showed an increase in length as the cell type* with the closest proximity to xylem cells*.
evidence: This is a description of model behavior when xylem stiffness is varied.

claim: A general decrease in the number of cells*, particularly of xylem cells*, was observed when xylem cell wall* stiffness was increased.
source: In addition, we observed a general decrease in the number of cells*, particularly of xylem cells* (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the computational model output shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The effect of decreased cell number when xylem stiffness is increased is explained by a 'physical' constraint generated by 'stiffer' xylem cells* acting on neighboring cambium cells* impairing their expansion and transformation into xylem*.
source: We explained this effect by a 'physical' constraint generated by 'stiffer' xylem cells* acting on neighboring cambium cells* impairing their expansion and, thus, their transformation into xylem* (Video 42, Video 43, Video 44, Video 45, Video 46, Video 47).
evidence: This is an inference based on the computational model output.

claim: Neither cell area nor cell length was affected in phloem cells* and the number of cambium cells* stayed constant when xylem stiffness was varied.
source: Importantly, neither cell area nor cell length was affected in phloem cells* and the number of cambium cells* stayed constant (Figure 5—figure supplement 1), suggesting that the general growth dynamics of the model and especially the behavior of cambium cells* was comparable under the different stiffness* regimes.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the computational model output shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Neither cell size* nor cell length* were impacted when epidermis* stiffness was varied.
source: When analyzing the same characteristics for the different epidermis* tissue regimes (Figure 5D, Video 48, Video 49, Video 50, Video 51, Video 52), we found that neither cell size* nor cell length* were impacted (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the computational model output shown in Figure 5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: A decrease in the number of cells* per simulation with increasing cell wall stiffness was found when epidermis* stiffness was varied, in particular phloem parenchyma* and phloem pole cells*.
source: Instead, we found a decrease in the number of cells* per simulation with increasing cell wall stiffness, in particular phloem parenchyma* and phloem pole cells*, as the increased resistance of the outer tissue boundary limited the overall tissue growth, resulting in less cells being produced in the outer parts of the tissue (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the computational model output shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: The increase of the xylem* to non-xylem cell wall* stiffness ratio produced a shift from more 'curved' lineages (R2 < 0.25) toward more radial lineages* (R2 > 0.75).
source: These comparisons showed that the increase of the xylem* to non-xylem cell wall* stiffness ratio produced a shift from more 'curved' lineages (R2 < 0.25) toward more radial lineages* (R2 > 0.75) (Figure 5G, Figure 5—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the computational model output shown in Figure 5G and Figure 5—figure supplement 3A.

claim: The effect of xylem stiffness on lineage radiality is attributed to an increased radial elongation of cambium cells* with increasing xylem stiffness* and the preferred cell division* along the shortest axis in VirtualLeaf.
source: We attributed this effect to an increased radial elongation of cambium cells* with increasing xylem stiffness* (Video 42, Video 43, Video 44, Video 45, Video 46, Video 47) and the preferred cell division* along the shortest axis in VirtualLeaf (Merks et al., 2011).
evidence: This is an inference based on the computational model output and the known behavior of VirtualLeaf.

claim: Implementing stiffness as a cell property produced coherent results in terms of the appearance of radial cell files* as an emergent property of xylem cell* wall stiffness.
source: Although the effect of xylem cell* stiffness on lineage radiality was not on all lineages, as a fraction of them remained less radially oriented even for high xylem stiffness (Figure 5G), implementing stiffness as a cell property therefore produced coherent results in terms of the appearance of radial cell files* as an emergent property of xylem cell* wall stiffness.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the computational model output shown in Figure 5G.

claim: The analysis of different epidermis cell wall stiffness did not show a clear change in the distribution of lineages in the range of analyzed stiffness regimes.
source: In contrast, the analysis of different epidermis cell wall stiffness did not show a clear change in the distribution of lineages in the range of analyzed stiffness regimes (Figure 5H, Figure 5—figure supplement 3B, Video 48, Video 49, Video 50, Video 51, Video 52) as increasing stiffness limited tissue growth and therefore the formation of cell lineages.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the computational model output shown in Figure 5H and Figure 5—figure supplement 3B.

claim: The results regarding stiffness effects remained consistent for both xylem* and epidermis* stiffness regimes when varying other parameters determining cell wall dynamics.
source: These results remained consistent for both xylem* and epidermis* stiffness regimes when varying other parameters determining cell wall dynamics, that is, the target length of cell wall elements and the yielding threshold for the introduction of new cell wall segments (Figure 5—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the computational model output shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 4.

claim: The rather simple cellular outline along the radial axes of plant organs, growth in only two dimensions, and the recent identification of central functional properties make radial plant growth an attractive target for a systematic approach to reveal its intriguing dynamics.
source: The rather simple cellular outline along the radial axes of plant organs, growth in only two dimensions, and the recent identification of central functional properties (Smetana et al., 2019; Miyashima et al., 2019; Shi et al., 2019) make radial plant growth an attractive target for a systematic approach to reveal its intriguing dynamics.
evidence: This is a rationale for the study supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The computational model represents a minimal framework required for radial plant growth using the VirtualLeaf framework.
source: Here, we developed a computational model representing a minimal framework required for radial plant growth using the VirtualLeaf framework (Merks et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a description of the study's approach supported by a citation.

claim: The model allows analyzing fundamental features of plant organ growth and integrates the PXY/CLE41 module as one central element for cambium patterning and maintenance.
source: Therefore, our model allows analyzing fundamental features of plant organ growth and integrates the PXY/CLE41 module as one central element for cambium patterning and maintenance.
evidence: This is a conclusion about the capabilities of the developed model.

claim: Using positional information mediated by morphogenetic gradients of diffusible chemicals to pattern growing structures is a classical concept in developmental biology.
source: Using positional information mediated by morphogenetic gradients of diffusible chemicals to pattern growing structures is a classical concept in developmental biology that has stirred a long history of fundamental debates (Green and Sharpe, 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: The PXY/CLE41 module was used to generate a gradient instructing cambium cells* to differentiate into xylem cells*, to proliferate, or to differentiate into phloem cells*.
source: Initially, we used the PXY/CLE41 module to generate such a gradient instructing cambium cells* to differentiate into xylem cells*, to proliferate, or to differentiate into phloem cells*.
evidence: This is a description of the modeling approach.

claim: Repression of cell division in the distal cambium was achieved by implementing an inhibitory feedback loop of PXY-signaling* on PXY* production.
source: Repression of cell division in the distal cambium was achieved by implementing an inhibitory feedback loop of PXY-signaling* on PXY* production.
evidence: This is a description of the modeling approach.

claim: The setup of the model was sufficient to maintain stable radial tissue organization during radial growth and established a maximum of cell division rates in the cambium center as observed by experimental means.
source: Altogether, this setup was already sufficient to maintain stable radial tissue organization during radial growth and established a maximum of cell division rates in the cambium center as observed by experimental means (Shi et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on model behavior and comparison with cited literature.

claim: Cambium organization and radial patterning of plant growth axes can be maintained by a distinct pattern of radially acting morphogens.
source: Thus, we conclude that cambium organization and radial patterning of plant growth axes can be maintained by a distinct pattern of radially acting morphogens.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the modeling results.

claim: Auxin's differential distribution seems to be rather a result of tissue patterning than being instructive for radial tissue organization.
source: Such a role was initially proposed for auxin whose differential distribution, however, seems to be rather a result of tissue patterning than being instructive for radial tissue organization (Bhalerao and Fischer, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The overall amount of proximal tissue production during radial plant growth did not depend on the PXY function.
source: In contrast to expected roles of the PXY pathway in xylem formation based on experiments during primary vascular development (Hirakawa et al., 2008; Hirakawa et al., 2010; Kondo et al., 2014), we observed that the overall amount of proximal tissue production during radial plant growth did not depend on the PXY function.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on experimental observations and comparison with cited literature.

claim: In contrast to a negative effect of PXY/CLE41 signaling on vessel formation in vascular bundles in leaves, vessel formation during radial plant growth is PXY/CLE41-independent.
source: Therefore, in contrast to a negative effect of PXY/CLE41 signaling on vessel formation in vascular bundles in leaves (Hirakawa et al., 2008; Kondo et al., 2014), vessel formation during radial plant growth is PXY/CLE41-independent.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on experimental observations and comparison with cited literature.

claim: Fiber formation is positively associated with the PXY/CLE41 module.
source: Instead, fiber formation is positively associated with the PXY/CLE41 module.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on experimental observations.

claim: Xylem formation is unlikely to be instructed by PXY/CLE41 signaling alone and additional signals are required.
source: These observations indicated that xylem formation is unlikely to be instructed by PXY/CLE41 signaling alone and that additional signals are required.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on experimental observations.

claim: PXY-deficiency leads to cambium disorganization in some regions of the hypocotyl, whereas in other areas, cambium anatomy is maintained.
source: Moreover, the application of markers visualizing cambium organization showed that PXY-deficiency leads to cambium disorganization in some regions of the hypocotyl, whereas in other areas, cambium anatomy is maintained.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on experimental observations.

claim: The pattern of cambium disorganization in pxy mutants may arise due to factors acting in parallel to PXY/CLE41 and which also carry spatial information.
source: Since such areas are regularly spaced, this pattern may arise due to factors acting in parallel to PXY/CLE41 and which also carry spatial information.
evidence: This is an inference based on experimental observations.

claim: PEAR transcription factors may act similarly to the PF* factor introduced in the model.
source: In contrast, PEAR transcription factors are phloem-derived and stimulate the proliferation of cambium stem cells presumably in a PXY/CLE41-independent manner (Miyashima et al., 2019) and, thus, may act similarly to the PF* factor we introduced in our model.
evidence: This is an inference based on cited literature and the model structure.

claim: The ERECTA/EPIDERMAL PATTERNING FACTOR-LIKE (ER/EPFL) receptor-ligand pathway acting in concert with the PXY/CLE41 module represents another candidate for playing a role in cambium organization.
source: The ERECTA/EPIDERMAL PATTERNING FACTOR-LIKE (ER/EPFL) receptor-ligand pathway acting in concert with the PXY/CLE41 module (Wang et al., 2019; Etchells et al., 2013) represents another candidate for playing such a role.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: CLE45 was recently proposed to be expressed in developing sieve elements and repress the establishment of sieve element identity in their immediate environment mediated by the RPK2 receptor protein.
source: In addition, CLE45 was recently proposed to be expressed in developing sieve elements, the conducting units of the phloem, and repress the establishment of sieve element identity in their immediate environment mediated by the RPK2 receptor protein (Gujas et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The PF* factor in the model combines features of phloem-derived molecules like PEARs, ER/EPFL, and CLE45.
source: The PF* factor in our model combines features of these phloem-derived molecules.
evidence: This is an inference based on the discussion of various phloem-derived factors.

claim: Early xylem cells have been identified to act as an organizing center of cambium patterning.
source: In addition to the phloem sending out instructive signals, early xylem cells have been identified to act as an organizing center of cambium patterning (Smetana et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The model ignored upstream regulation of postulated factors like PXY* or CLE41*, which depends on positional information which could be mediated in plants by auxin or cytokinin signaling.
source: Although this finding seems to be at odds with our claim that phloem-derived signals are sufficient for cambium organization, it is important to consider that we ignored, for example, upstream regulation of postulated factors like PXY* or CLE41*, which obviously depends on positional information which could be mediated in plants by auxin or cytokinin signaling (Bishopp et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a discussion of model limitations supported by a citation.

claim: The model ignored organizing effects of signaling longitudinally to cross-sections as it can be expected for polar auxin transport in the context of cambium activity or xylem formation.
source: For simplicity, we also ignored organizing effects of signaling longitudinally to cross-sections as it can, for example, be expected for polar auxin transport (Bennett et al., 2016; Ibañes et al., 2009; Fàbregas et al., 2015) in the context of cambium activity or xylem formation.
evidence: This is a discussion of model limitations supported by citations.

claim: The establishment of 3D models will be crucial and essential for addressing the aspect of longitudinal signaling.
source: Although being considerably more complex, the establishment of 3D models will be crucial and essential for addressing this aspect.
evidence: This is a discussion of future directions.

claim: The transition from the initially bisymmetric tissue conformation to a concentric tissue organization as it occurs in hypocotyls and roots was deliberately excluded from the model.
source: In this context, it is interesting to note that we deliberately excluded the transition from the initially bisymmetric tissue conformation to a concentric tissue organization as it occurs in hypocotyls and roots (Smetana et al., 2019; Sankar et al., 2014) from our model.
evidence: This is a discussion of model scope supported by citations.

claim: The rationale for excluding the transition to concentric tissue organization was that the complex change in tissue anatomy required more assumptions and would have spoiled the advantages of a relatively simple anatomy.
source: Our rationale was that the rather complex change in tissue anatomy from a primary to a secondary conformation in the hypocotyl required more assumptions in our model and would have spoiled the advantages of a relatively simple anatomy for generating a cell-based computational model.
evidence: This is a discussion of the rationale for model design choices.

claim: The differences in primary anatomy of shoots and roots before the onset of radial plant growth would have required different cellular outlines for both cases and would have hampered the generality of the approach.
source: Moreover, the differences in primary anatomy of shoots and roots before the onset of radial plant growth (Smetana et al., 2019; Sehr et al., 2010) would have required different cellular outlines for both cases and, thus, would have hampered the generality of our approach.
evidence: This is a discussion of the rationale for model design choices supported by citations.

claim: The front of cambium domains is very stable, almost perfectly circular, in planta but this is not the case for the computational simulations.
source: Interestingly, the front of cambium domains is very stable, that is, almost perfectly circular, in planta but this is not the case for our computational simulations.
evidence: This is a comparison between model behavior and observed plant anatomy.

claim: Instability in the computational models is due to local noise in the cellular pattern leading to differential diffusion of chemicals* with respect to their radial position and to a progressive deviation of domains from a perfect circle.
source: We believe that instability in the computational models is due to local noise in the cellular pattern leading to differential diffusion of chemicals* with respect to their radial position and to a progressive deviation of domains from a perfect circle.
evidence: This is an inference based on model behavior.

claim: A corrective mechanism ensuring front stability in planta is not implemented in the models due to the absence of a good indication in planta.
source: Such a deviation seems to be corrected by an unknown mechanism in planta but such a corrective mechanism is due to the absence of a good indication in planta not implemented in our models.
evidence: This is a discussion of model limitations.

claim: 'Gaps' in the cambium domain in pxy mutants are already present at early stages of development, arguing against the possibility that the pxy anatomy is caused by increased front instability.
source: Analyses of wt and pxy lines at different stages (Figure 3—figure supplement 1, Figure 3—figure supplement 2, Figure 3—figure supplement 3, Figure 3—figure supplement 4) revealed 'gaps' in the cambium domain already at early stages of pxy development arguing against the possibility that the pxy anatomy is caused by increased front instability.
evidence: This is an inference based on experimental observations shown in supplementary figures.

claim: The model now allows to test ideas like directional movement of chemicals or stabilizing communication between cells during cambium activity.
source: Although a corrective mechanism ensuring front stability in planta is difficult to predict, our model now allows to test respective ideas like directional movement of chemicals or stabilizing communication between cells during cambium activity.
evidence: This is a discussion of future applications of the model.

claim: Increasing epidermis* 'stiffness' increased circularity of the growing organ*, which may be administered by the periderm.
source: In this context, it is interesting that increasing epidermis* 'stiffness' increased circularity of the growing organ*, which may be administered by the periderm (Serra et al., 2022), the protective cell layers that we did not consider in our model.
evidence: This is an inference based on model behavior and cited literature.

claim: Microtubules, turgor pressure, and cell wall composition are central factors in how cell mechanical properties influence cell and tissue morphogenesis.
source: Current research on plant mechanical biology indicates how cell mechanical properties influence cell and tissue morphogenesis. Microtubules, turgor pressure, and cell wall composition are central factors in this regard (Sapala et al., 2018; Altartouri et al., 2019).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Due to the geometric constraints in a radially growing plant axis, it becomes challenging to uncouple factors like microtubules, turgor pressure, and cell wall composition experimentally and establish the impact of one factor on organ patterning during radial plant growth.
source: Due to the geometric constraints in a radially growing plant axis, it becomes challenging to uncouple these factors experimentally and establish the impact of one factor on organ patterning during radial plant growth.
evidence: This is a rationale for the computational modeling approach.

claim: By expanding VirtualLeaf to allow for the integration of cell-type-specific wall stiffness, the spectrum of potential modeling approaches was fundamentally increased.
source: By expanding VirtualLeaf to allow for the integration of cell-type-specific wall stiffness, we fundamentally increased the spectrum of potential modeling approaches.
evidence: This is a description of the methodological contribution of the study.

claim: It is now possible to simulate and analyze the dynamics of auxin or brassinosteroid-mediated cell wall loosening.
source: In particular, since cell wall stiffness is accessible by the cellular model throughout simulations, it is now possible to simulate and analyze, for example, the dynamics of auxin or brassinosteroid-mediated cell wall loosening (Majda and Robert, 2018; Caesar et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a discussion of future applications of the model supported by citations.

claim: By modulating exclusively cellular 'stiffness,' a hypothesis was developed on how inter-tissue forces influence stem cell behavior not only cell autonomously, but also in a non-cell-autonomous manner.
source: In our cambium model, by modulating exclusively cellular 'stiffness,' we were able to computationally simplify the 'physical' properties and, thereby, develop a hypothesis how inter-tissue forces influence stem cell behavior not only cell autonomously, but also in a non-cell-autonomous manner.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the modeling results.

claim: The model recapitulates the qualitative and quantitative variation in radial plant growth on multiple levels, found in different mutants or when comparing different dicotyledonous species.
source: Taken together, we envision that the model presented in this study recapitulates the qualitative and quantitative variation in radial plant growth on multiple levels, found in different mutants or when comparing different dicotyledonous species (Spicer and Groover, 2010).
evidence: This is a discussion of the model's potential applications supported by a citation.

claim: Remarkable features like the establishment of concentric cambium rings often found in the order of Caryophyllales or 'phloem wedges' found in the Bignonieae genus may be recapitulated by adjusting the model's parameters values or by introducing additional factors.
source: Remarkable features like the establishment of concentric cambium rings often found in the order of Caryophyllales (Carlquist, 2007) or 'phloem wedges' found in the Bignonieae genus (Pace et al., 2009) may be recapitulated by adjusting the model's parameters values or by introducing additional factors.
evidence: This is a discussion of the model's potential applications supported by citations.

claim: In the future, the model may help to predict targets of environmental stimuli inducing changes of cambium activity like seasonal changes or mechanical perturbation, allowing the generation of testable hypotheses.
source: In the future, the model may help to predict targets of environmental stimuli inducing changes of cambium activity like seasonal changes (Bhalerao and Fischer, 2017) or mechanical perturbation (Gerttula et al., 2015), allowing the generation of testable hypotheses.
evidence: This is a discussion of future applications of the model supported by citations.

claim: The dynamic model will be a useful tool for investigating a process not possible to observe in real time and partly develops over exceptionally long periods.
source: Thus, our dynamic model will be a useful tool for investigating a process not possible to observe in real time and partly develops over exceptionally long periods.
evidence: This is a conclusion about the utility of the model.
